entries.title: Nothing’s New Headphone (1) Pro Are Made for the Studio
entries.summary: With three drivers in each ear and tuning from Metropolis Studios, Nothing wants its new $399 cans to shine in the studio while also making your commute more musical.
entries.content:
The Headphone (1) Pro is Nothing's newest pair of cans, the company announced on Monday at an evening event in New York City. The headphones resemble Nothing’s first-ever over-ear headphones that debuted last summer, though the design and fit have been refined. The key change, though, is audio quality.

Instead of a single dynamic driver producing the sound in each earcup, Nothing has outfitted the Headphone (1) Pro with three drivers for each ear. Most headphones use a single 40-mm dynamic driver, so a single speaker ends up handling the bass, mids, and treble of your tracks. That can cause some muddiness and distortion. Adding more drivers—one for each specific frequency spectrum—gives the sound more room to stretch out and sparkle.

There’s a 40-mm bass dynamic driver to handle the low end. Then there’s a precision dynamic driver to tackle the midrange sounds like vocals, pianos, and guitars. The company says this driver will render those “S” and “T” sounds with more detail. Finally, there's the treble driver for the highs. Nothing’s driver uses xMEMS technology, which relies on a silicon diaphragm that should make transients—sharp bursts like a cymbal hit or a spiky synth stab—sound clearer.

All of these drivers working together should produce richer sound that’s more detailed overall. Every headphone maker claims their gadget produces the best sound on the market, but at least Nothing has attempted some technical feats here to try to convince you.

What's neat is you can see elements of the triple-driver architecture on the sides of the headphones—Nothing has added a couple of 9H Panda glass panels so you can peep the tech inside. The rest of the headphones are largely aluminum with titanium accents.

You'll no doubt worry about cracking that glass; Nothing claims that it is “shatter- and scratch-resistant," but Philipp Von Lintel, associate principal industrial designer at Nothing, says the glass had to survive durability tests 18 times from a drop of more than 1 meter. Also, the glass construction shouldn't affect repairability much—repair technicians can heat the glass from the outside to remove it and access the internal chamber for fixes. “Even if you crack it, there's a plastic film that keeps the chamber still working,” Von Lintel tells WIRED.

The Headphone (1) Pro is slightly lighter (by 2 grams) than the Headphone (1), with a wider headband and thicker padding, though battery life isn't as long, down to 68 hours with active noise canceling turned off versus 80. It has an IP52 dust- and water-resistance rating, so keep the hood of your rain jacket raised on rainy days.

Almost every gadget maker tosses the “Pro” moniker in the product name to justify a few extra features and a price bump. Yes, the Headphone (1) Pro cost $399, a $100 bump over the standard Headphone (1), but Nothing claims it is specifically catering to not just the average consumer who wants better sound, but also recording artists and audio professionals who work in the studio.

The company is including a feature that activates a flat equalization (EQ) mode—something mix engineers and audio producers prefer when they’re working—that’s triggered by a physical button on the headphones. Nothing collaborated with Metropolis Studio, a pro recording studio, to make the EQ features. There's even a “Studio B” Dynamic Spatial Audio mode that simulates Metropolis' mixing room, and four other Custom EQ profiles, like Concert Hall or Club. And yes, there’s a 3.5-mm jack so you can plug in (or stick with hi-res wireless or USB-C).

Charlie Smith, Nothing’s chief brand officer, says people will want these headphones for their commute to work. “That's fine, but people are making music on the go and need studio-level sound wherever they are," he says.

Nothing also claims the headphones have the best active noise cancellation it’s ever shipped, thanks to the use of 10 microphones to filter out ambient sounds. (Apple's AirPods Max, for comparison, use eight.)

“To us, this is a flagship product where we're able to showcase what we can do," Smith says. “It also helps elevate us as a brand.”

Sadly, they don’t fold up. Instead, Nothing is following Apple’s lead by including a bra-like carry case to keep the cans protected.

They'll officially hit store shelves on September 29—not only on Nothing's online store and Amazon, but also nationwide in Best Buy stores across North America.

entries.title: Shark’s NeverChange Air Purifier Is Nearly Half Off Right Now
entries.summary: Shark and other top air purifier brands are on discount ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.
entries.content:
The Shark NeverChange air purifier is already affordable, but this 40 percent discount makes it an even better deal. Like other models in Shark's NeverChange line, this model boasts a five-year filter lifespan when used and cleaned as recommended, potentially saving hundreds of dollars on replacement filters.

Shark has a few other WIRED-tested models on sale, which I've listed below. Although Amazon Prime Big Deal Days haven’t formally started yet (see our early deal coverage here), several popular air purifier brands, like Levoit and Coway, also have models already on sale. Be sure to read on to find which on-sale air purifier is best for your home.

Check out our guides to keeping your home's air quality in tip-top shape, including the Best Air Purifiers, Best Multiuse Air Purifiers, Best Fans, and Best Air Quality Monitors.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

The Shark NeverChange Air Purifier exchanges the air nearly five times per hour in spaces up to 130 square feet, making it a good fit for small rooms such as bedrooms, bathrooms, and laundry rooms. It has a long-lasting HEPA filter that captures fine particles, and an activated carbon filter that traps odors and gases. As mentioned above, one standout feature of this budget-friendly purifier is its filter, which can last up to five years with regular cleaning and use on energy-saving settings. It’s also a good option for pet owners: There's a small cartridge filled with a fragrance pod to help offset pet odors and keep the air smelling fresh. This makes it ideal for rooms where you store your cat's litter box or have your dog's crate.

If you want a compact air purifier that's ideal for smaller rooms, can operate close to a wall, and uses useful odor-neutralizing technology, the Shark NeverChange Air Purifier is a solid choice. At nearly $100 off, this discounted model is ideal for pet parents looking to fight odors and dander.

entries.title: Boox Announces the Picco, Its Smallest E-Reader Ever (2026)
entries.summary: The Boox Picco is a palm-sized e-reader with a 4-inch screen, strong support for different ebook formats, and digital utility tools.
entries.content:
While smartphones won't stop getting bigger, e-readers seem to be getting smaller. Boox has been at the forefront with one of the most popular small e-readers, the Boox Palma, and now it is adding an even smaller model.

Boox announced the Picco, with preorders opening today. Its screen is just under 4 inches (3.97 to be exact), making it about the size of a playing card. It's even smaller than the Xteink X4 Pro I tested earlier this year, which has a 4.3-inch screen (but just slightly larger than the 3.7-inch Xteink X3), and considerably smaller than the upcoming Boox Palma 3's 6.19-inch screen. I liked the size of the Xteink in my hand, but navigating the interface and getting books were challenging, so I'm excited to see another option in that smaller size from a maker with more accessible ebooks (though still not as convenient as a Kindle or Kobo with their built-in stores).

The Picco will cost $100 and is expected to ship in November. I'll be testing it soon, but in the meantime, here are the details if you've been eyeing a tiny e-reader.

An E-Reader for Productivity

The Boox Picco has a monochrome screen with a resolution of 235 pixels per inch and an adjustable front light that switches between warm- and cool-toned lighting. The microSD card slot supports up to 2 TB of flash memory storage (a 16 GB card is included). There are both a touchscreen and physical page-turning controls, thanks to the buttons on the side of the device. The case has a magnetic ring so you can attach it to the back of a smartphone, though I'll have to see how well it fits when I test it, as I had mixed results attaching an Xteink to my phone due to both fit and magnet strength.

Boox says the Picco will have a streamlined operating system focused on reading and digital utility tools. It's also the first in what Boox calls its Tiles lineup, which is how you'll access ebooks on this device. You can also use web and USB-C file transfers (the Picco has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity) to get ebooks onto the Picco. The Picco also has the Pomodoro, Todo, and Countdown apps, so you can use it as both an e-reader and a productivity gadget—handy, and a bigger motivation to keep it attached to the back of your phone even when you aren't reading.

I'm intrigued to see it in action. Boox's most popular e-reader could become the Picco over the Palma 3, but we'll have to wait for both devices to become available to see which is the better buy. Stay tuned for my reviews of both when they come out.

entries.title: Meta-Led Anti-Terrorism Group Faces Mass Resignation of Expert Advisers
entries.summary: Meta and other tech giants are pushing through structural changes at the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism that outside researchers allege will weaken oversight of an already embattled consortium.
entries.content:
Six of the nine independent experts on the advisory board of the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism—a consortium run by several of the biggest US tech companies—resigned on Monday, according to a letter seen by WIRED and interviews with four of the people.

The tensions between the independent advisory committee and the GIFCT date back to an email the counterterrorism and free speech experts received in July from Meta’s Nell McCarthy, a vice president overseeing content policy. For years, the group had advised the GIFCT on how to prevent platforms from becoming havens for the radical organizations and individuals blamed for some of the world’s worst mass violence.

But McCarthy wrote that while the consortium welcomed the experts’ insights on violent trends, it no longer desired their scrutiny on the effectiveness of Big Tech’s efforts to curtail violence. Meta and other leaders wanted to “refresh” the 6-year-old independent advisory committee the experts sat on, she wrote. Meta serves as chair of GIFCT’s operating board this year, giving it outsized influence over policy changes, though other companies on the panel must ultimately approve.

New additions to the rotating advisory committee had previously been elected by current members; under the plan laid out in July, they would instead be picked by tech companies. The committee would be barred from weighing in on key topics such as the consortium’s performance and making recommendations together as a group. Its role as a watchdog would be neutered, advisers believed.

In their resignation letter, the departing members of the committee wrote that their appeals against the plan had been “ignored” and that, in turn, they had “lost confidence in the GIFCT’s ability to deliver effectively on its founding mission” to prevent terrorists from exploiting online services. “We all know that a body that cannot scrutinise, take a position, or evaluate is not an advisory body at all,” the letter stated. “It is decoration and accountability theatre.”

Meta deferred comment on the resignations to the GIFCT. An unsigned statement sent to WIRED by a GIFCT spokesperson on behalf of the consortium’s leadership and the Meta-chaired operating board says the proposed changes have been “informed by several rounds of feedback” and are not yet final. They came out of discussions on “how to more effectively engage civil society and governments for substantive input” as “multi-stakeholderism is a core principle” for the GIFCT.

The consortium has about 35 members; other long-time board members include Microsoft and YouTube. A small staff alerts members to violent content, helps them exchange threat intelligence, and commissions research on countering extremism. While the coordination has helped some platforms combat problematic content, critics believe the group isn’t living up to its potential.

A WIRED investigation in 2024 uncovered several issues with GIFCT, including Meta delaying TikTok’s membership bid and poor relations between the companies at the helm and the unpaid independent advisory body. It also revealed failures in the tip-sharing database the consortium oversees to coordinate takedowns of problematic content.

The dismantling of the advisory group threatens to deteriorate the organization’s work further at a time when balancing free expression and online safety has become more challenging. Generative AI tools have simplified content creation but imposed limited guardrails.

Extremist content, including some that is now AI-generated, that promotes organizations such as Islamic State remains a persistent issue. Newer nihilistic collectives have turned to AI-supported scams such as sexploitation to coerce young victims into carrying out violence and abuse. Several AI chatbots have been accused of facilitating violence.

“A Shame”

The experts who resigned include university researchers and representatives of civil society organizations. They had agreed with McCarthy on the need for changes to improve the results of the decade-old anti-terrorism consortium. But they believe the proposal, which could be finalized soon, amounts to a step backward.

“There won’t be critical voices raising concerns about what GIFCT is doing or is not doing,” one of the departing experts says. “It may seem politically convenient for them to abolish the independent advisory committee, but they are going to regret it in the longer term.”

Another calls it “a shame” that the tech companies “instead of engaging and building better evaluation and transparency are pursuing a rollback of independence that was already weak to begin with.”

Both of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retaliation from the Trump administration, which has denied visas to people it believes are working to unfairly censor online content, and Republicans in Congress, who have been investigating supposed censorship groups. While the GIFCT hasn’t been targeted, both it and an adviser’s organization were mentioned in a February report from the House Judiciary Committee.

In a meeting soon after, the advisory committee questioned consortium leaders, including from Meta, about their plans to operate in what appeared to be a fraught political environment for content moderation, according to two of the advisers present. The committee didn’t get clear answers, the people say, but got pushback for raising questions considered beyond its purview. About three months later came McCarthy’s July email.

WIRED couldn’t immediately learn why four of the expert advisers did not join the others in resigning. The committee also includes representatives from the UN and a handful of governments such as Canada and the EU, and it’s unclear whether any of them will also exit. But last Friday, the entire panel of 17 members sent a letter, seen by WIRED, to McCarthy disagreeing with her plan to curtail their group’s independence and input.

When the consortium formed the advisory committee in 2020, its then-executive director Nick Rasmussen said he had encouraged many of the inaugural members to be “the conscience of the organization” and “if necessary, to call bullshit.”

In public reports, the committee has credited its input for helping grow the consortium, expand the types of tips shared, and increase the transparency of its work. But the people who resigned believe they were often consulted too late to meaningfully influence most of the consortium’s projects.

The proposal calls for transitioning the body’s name from “committee” to “community” and forbidding it from evaluating the consortium’s governance, budget, operations, and the work of individual member companies, according to the resignation letter.

New experts recruited to the “community,” regardless of who appoints them, will quickly come to the same conclusion as those who resigned, one of the people says. “We will be on a merry-go round. It may just be that the GIFCT model has run its course.”

entries.title: These Extremists Are Running for Election in November
entries.summary: With the threat of political violence at unprecedented levels, state and federal GOP candidates are openly sharing racist, pro-militia, anti-vaccine, sexist, antisemitic, and secessionist views.
entries.content:
There are five weeks left until the midterm elections, and extremism is on the ballot in much of the US. A WIRED review of candidates running for statewide and federal positions in November, along with exclusive data on candidates running for state-level positions, reveals hundreds of Republican candidates who openly express virulently hateful ideologies, share racist content online, have close ties to white supremacist and antisemitic figures, and are members of far-right groups online. President Donald Trump and his administration have openly embraced, endorsed and defended many of these candidates.

At a local level, over 500 candidates running for state legislator positions in November are members of far-right groups on Facebook that promote militias, gun rights, and Christian nationalism, according to data collected by the Institute for Research and Education on Human Rights and shared with WIRED.

While many extremist candidates—such as groyper James Fishback and antisemitic influencer Dan Bilzerian— didn’t make it through GOP primaries, many made it to the general election, and a number of them are expected to win.

“The candidates are taking a page out of the Trump administration’s playbook,” Luke Baumgartner, a former research fellow at George Washington University’s Program on Extremism, tells WIRED. Baumgartner claims that many of the candidates running in November have been inspired by those in the White House. “In essence, the executive branch has handed them a permission slip to say and do what would have been unthinkable during the George W. Bush, McCain, or [Mitt] Romney eras of the GOP,” he says.

Extremist rhetoric has led to real world political threats. In 2025, terrorism and targeted violence incidents rose 19 percent compared to 2024, according to researchers at the University of Maryland; the US Capitol Police reported an increase in “threat assessment cases” against members of Congress for the third year in a row, with a 58 percent increase from 2024; and the US Marshals Service documented threats against almost 400 judges, a roughly 5 percent increase from the previous year.

Here are five races involving candidates who have shared extremist ideologies or have close ties to extremist figures, that WIRED is watching ahead of the November midterms.

The Texas Railroad Commissioner Race

Bo French, the GOP candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner, is so extreme that Republican strategist Karl Rove has said he would vote for a Democrat rather than supporting a “bigot.”

Earlier this month, French posted racist comments about students celebrating at a University of Texas at Austin football game. “Like bodycam footage exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners,” French wrote alongside a picture of students of South Asian descent celebrating a victory over Ohio State. “It’s everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine.” (Former Border Patrol leader Greg Bovino wrote in reply, “Mass deportations will solve it in very short order.”)

While many Republicans, including senator John Cornyn from Texas, criticized French for his post and called on him to take it down, French instead doubled down, telling a conservative radio host that while he didn’t “have anything against the people specifically in that picture,” he wanted to “prioritize Americans.”

This wasn’t the first controversy for the candidate: French has previously called for the removal of 100 million people from America, including US citizens, and repeatedly used homophobic slurs.

The Texas Railroad Commissioner is an incredibly powerful position that has no role in regulating railroads, but instead oversees the state’s oil and gas industries, which in Texas drill more oil and other hydrocarbons than the rest of the US combined. The role will also be critical to deciding how the burgeoning data center industry in Texas will be powered.

New polling this week suggests French, who has not been publicly endorsed by Trump, is a slim favorite to win the seat.

Arizona’s 5th Congressional District Race

Mark Lamb, the GOP nominee for Arizona’s 5th district congressional race, is a former sheriff and reality TV star. He has deep ties to paramilitary groups, anti-immigration organizations, and the far-right constitutional sheriffs movement.

Lamb has protested Covid lockdowns and vaccine mandates, expressed support for the “stop the steal” movement,” and sympathized with the rioters who stormed the Capitol on January 6. He is in favor of private militias and even authorized the formation of a civilian posse while serving as sheriff of Pinal County in response to Black Lives Matter protests in 2020. He is a regular on right wing podcasts, including those hosted by white nationalists and conspiracy theorists.

Lamb, who is supported by Trump and conservative student organization Turning Point USA, won his primary despite accusations of multiple sex scandals. When one woman threatened to expose him, a Facebook account featuring an avatar of Lamb’s face threatened to use Arizona’s revenge porn law against her.

Lamb is almost certain to be elected in the deeply red district that includes Phoenix.

Texas’ 23rd Congressional District Race

Brandon Herrera, who rose to fame as a so-called “guntuber,” is running for Congress in Texas in the district that represents Uvalde. Incumbent GOP congressman Tony Gonzales resigned after admitting to an affair, making Herrera the GOP candidate.

Herrera has a very long history of sharing sexist, racist, and antisemitic opinions. He has said that a Nazi-era submachine gun was “the original ghetto blaster” and “Hitler’s street sweeper.” He has compared feminists’ weight to whales, elephants, and nuclear bombs and described liberal women discussing guns as “both fat and wrong.” While talking about Shannon Watts, the gun control activist who set up Moms Demand Action following the Sandy Hook school shooting, Herrera said: “The fact that you kept your cum trophy doesn’t make you any less wrong about the dumb shit that you say.”

“HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN,” Trump wrote about Herrera in a Truth Social post in March.

When questioned about Herrera’s opinions of women, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson dismissed them as part of his online “persona.” Johnson also called Herrera a “very serious candidate” and a “very thoughtful guy.”

Herrera is in a tight race with Democrat nominee Katy Padilla Stout.

Georgia’s Senate Race

Mike Collins, the Trump-backed GOP senate candidate in Georgia, is running against Democratic incumbent Jon Ossoff.

Collins has spent a large part of his campaign battling accusations that he supports or is indifferent to white supremacy and antisemitism—not because of anything he has said, but because of who he has surrounded himself with. In May, NOTUS reported that former Collins staffer William Paul (son of Kentucky senator Rand Paul) hurled antisemitic insults at representative Mike Lawler from New York while both were at a bar.

Later the same month, Slate revealed that Collins’ then chief-of-staff, Kip Talley, was in a group chat with known white supremacists like Nick Fuentes and Richard Spencer. In the texts, Talley said he was working to help Charles “Chuck” Johnson, a Holocaust denier who has been accused of (and denied) being a white nationalist, who was in jail at the time as he was in contempt of court as part of a racketeering lawsuit. Talley told Slate that he was concerned about an “acquaintance I have known for years was being mistreated in custody and denied basic medical care.”

In July, CNN revealed that Collins’ son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, is a social media influencer who has shared antisemitic content and Nazi imagery. And finally, last month, the Washington Post revealed that a former intern and contractor for his PAC had shared images on X of a swastika and an image of himself in what appear to be KKK robes.

Collins has repeatedly said that he condemns antisemitism and hate speech of any kind. He also secured Trump’s endorsement earlier this month.

Polling shows Ossoff comfortably leading Collins in the general election.

Florida’s State House’s 10th District Race

Marshall Rawson, a 34-year old citrus farmer and GOP activist, was the surprise winner of the Republican primary in August for the Florida legislature’s 10th District House race.

Talking Points Memo revealed this month that Rawson marched at the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville and was pictured close to the neo-Nazi who later would drive his car into a crowd of protesters, killing Heather Heyer.

On social media, Rawson has repeatedly posted racist remarks. He has also suggested that gay people should be criminally charged and possibly executed. He has been associated with the racist and antisemitic League of the South movement, which seeks secession for southern states from the US.

Talking Points Memo revealed that his campaign is getting donations from the daughter of former KKK leader David Duke, along with another individual who marched in Charlottesville and admitted to organizing a birthday party for Duke.

There is no public polling available for the race, but the district leans heavily red, with Republicans winning the seat by a 48-point margin in 2024.

entries.title: Best External Hard Drives (2026): SanDisk, Samsung, and More
entries.summary: Need an ultrafast drive for video editing or a rugged option to back up your photos in the field? We’ve got a solution for every situation.
entries.content:
I know you'll back up all those photos on your phone someday, but you should do it today. Just get a little external or portable hard drive, plug it into your phone, and make a backup. Trust me: It's so much easier than trying to recover them after your phone dies.

Ideally, choose a solid-state drive whenever possible—they're fast and durable. But which SSD, you ask? Great question. I’ve tested dozens so far, using all kinds of devices and operating systems, to figure out what works best and where. But don't dismiss a traditional hard disk drive (HDD), as it's still useful and cheaper for backing up everything on your computer. These are my top picks for the most common use cases.

A word of warning: The AI race and its accompanying flurry of memory-hungry data centers are driving prices sky-high, with no end in sight. Drives in this guide have quadrupled in price in the past six months. For example, 8-TB SSDs are selling for more than a new MacBook Air, which has itself gone up $200 to help cover surging memory costs.

Check out our other guides, including How to Back Up and Move Your Photos Between Services, How to Back Up Your Digital Life, and How to Back Up Your iPhone.

Updated September 2026: I’ve added a SanDisk SSD made for NAS systems and a Satechi drive enclosure, removed some sold-out drives, and added a few notes on how AI is still ruining everything. I've also updated prices and links throughout. Note that memory prices are extremely volatile and could change after publication.

Best for Desktop Hard Drive

If you have a lot of data to back up and don't want to spend a fortune, the Western Digital Elements desktop drive is your best bet. I have been using a variation of the Elements desktop hard drive to back up my data for more than a decade. These drives are big and require external power, but they’re some of the cheapest and most reliable I’ve used. This is one instance where it makes sense to invest in an HDD, especially since you should not need to access the data frequently, which puts stress on the moving parts.

Transfer speeds are not off the charts—the Elements drive I tested scored 120 megabytes per second (MB/s) for sequential writes on Windows—but you should ideally run backups overnight, and even at these speeds the average PC backup will be done by morning. These drives use USB-C 3.2, and I’ve had no problem using them with Windows, macOS, or Linux.

Storage options range from 1 TB to 26 terabytes. Just check the prices; sometimes you can get a 10- or even 12-TB drive for not much more than the 8-terabyte version. I have not seen a huge difference between the Elements line and the brand’s higher-end My Book drives, and the basic Elements drive is sufficient for most people.

  • Seagate Desktop Drive 8000 for approximately $300 (8 TB): Seagate is also a reliable drive maker. It never hurts to have more backups, and when you make multiple backups, I recommend using drives from different brands, since that reduces the chance they'll both fail at the same time. This one is discontinued but still available, and it did extremely well in our speed tests.

Best for Backing Up Your Phone

Micron has discontinued its Crucial brand when it wound down its consumer business. While the products are being phased out, you can still find them for sale. In fact, it may be the best way to score a reliable SSD from a reputable company at a reasonable price.

Crucial’s X9 Pro hits the sweet spot of speed and portability, making it the best way to back up your phone. Sure, cloud-based backups are great, but local backups are fast and offer more privacy. These Crucial drives are tiny, about half the size of a deck of cards, and weigh a mere 1.3 ounces. They’ll connect to just about anything. I tested the X9 Pro with iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, and Linux, and I never ran into any issues.

When it comes to speed, the X9 Pro claims symmetrical read and write speeds of 1,050 MB/s. I actually consistently got higher speeds, up to 1,110 MB/s for read and 1,100 MB/s for write. That puts the X9 Pro at the top of the pack for portable drive speed.

I’ve been using the X9 Pro for over a year now, and while I can’t speak to its long-term survival rate yet, I have tested Crucial's X6 and X8 drives for over three years without issue, if that gives you an indication of the X9 Pro's potential. There is also the X10 Pro drive (approximately $360), which offers even faster speeds. The X10 Pro delivers on its promise of 2,100 MB/s (I got it up to 2,050 MB/s). If your hardware supports it, the X10 Pro is worth the extra money, but for most people the X9 Pro will work just fine.

Best for Backups on the Go

I love Western Digital’s My Passport series for on-the-road backups. The Ultra version of this HDD uses a standard USB-C cable (many portable HDDs still use the USB Micro-B connector) and is available in sizes up to 6 TB. It’s not the thinnest drive on the market, but it’s less than an inch thick and solid enough that I never worry about tossing it in my bag. (That said, it is a spinning drive without a rugged enclosure, so don’t literally toss it.) I also like that the corners are nicely rounded and there are no screws or anything else that will snag on fabric in your bag.

Performance is good for a mechanical hard drive. I tested it with CrystalDiskMark on Windows, AmorphousDiskMark on macOS, and KDiskMark on Linux, then averaged the results to get 121 MB/s read and 115 MB/s write. The Ultra delivers higher write speeds than many similar portable drives, especially on small blocks of data, like transferring photos from an SD card via a laptop. And it's plenty fast enough to run a daily backup in your hotel room overnight.

The 256-bit AES encryption helps keep data secure, making it ideal for travelers and road warriors. Versions are available for Windows and macOS; they are formatted accordingly and include software for a particular operating system. Make sure you get the right model for your laptop, but you can reformat it for whatever OS you use (you can download and reinstall the manufacturer's backup software or use the tools built into the OS).

  • Seagate Portable External Hard Drive for $190 (4 TB): Seagate's answer to the Ultra is slightly thinner and more pocketable (does anyone really carry a spinning drive in their pocket though?), but write speeds were slightly slower in my testing, and there are no encryption features. That said, if you can catch this one on sale for less than the Ultra, it's worth getting.
  • Western Digital Elements Portable HDD for $165 (2 TB): This drive is slightly thinner than our top pick but feels flimsier in my experience. Speeds are a tad slower, but you can grab one for far less than the Ultra series drives.

A More Rugged Spinning Drive

A quick history lesson. G-Technology was a high-end storage drive maker. Fabrik acquired it; Hitachi bought Fabrik; and then Hitachi became part of Western Digital. Throughout these transitions, the companies retained the well-regarded G-Drive lineup of hard drives. After WD bought SanDisk, it shifted the G-Drive to the new SanDisk Professional brand. Fast-forward to 2025, and WD spun off SanDisk (now spelled Sandisk, if you're still following) as its own company focused on flash memory products. WD, however, kept the G-Drive brand for a series of high-performance drives.

That brings us to the G-Drive ArmorATD, a solid, semi-rugged external hard disk drive that doesn't (currently) cost as much as some others in its class. We tested it when it was part of the SanDisk Professional division, and you're likely to still find it branded as such. Somewhat unique among external drives, it supports the macOS-friendly HFS+ format out of the box, making it plug-and-play with Apple’s Time Machine backup system. You can still use it with Windows, but you’ll just need to reformat it to exFAT (likewise, when testing on Linux, I formatted it to ext4).

The ArmorATD is compact for a spinning drive, measuring 3.4 by 5.1 inches and less than an inch thick. A removable black rubberized sleeve cushions the drive, and the enclosure is a silverish-gray on the top and bottom. One end has a cover that protects a USB-C port with a USB 3.1 Gen 1 interface (which works with Thunderbolt 3 or higher ports on Macs). The ArmorATD comes with two cables: one USB-C to USB-C and one USB-C to USB-A.

I describe this drive as semi-rugged because it’s a spinning drive, which makes it more vulnerable to bumps and bruises, but it's designed to sustain drops of up to 3.3 feet, and it has an IP54 rating, which means it’ll stand up to splashes, but it can't be submerged in water.

The ArmorATD managed a read speed of 133 MB/s, just below the claimed 135 MB/s and a little faster than the WD Passport Ultra above. In all my testing, I haven't seen a huge difference among similar spinning drives (most 5,400-rpm drives score around 120 to 130 MB/s), and you’re unlikely to notice much difference in real-world tasks. Some users complain online that G-Drives aren't as good as they were before Western Digital acquired them, but I didn't have issues during my review. If you want something a little more rugged, the G-Drive ArmorATD is a great option at a reasonable price. I tested the 2-TB model, but options range from 1 TB to 6 TB.

Best Thunderbolt 5 Drive

The LaCie Rugged Pro5 is currently one of the most eye-wateringly expensive SSDs on the market, but it is an amazingly fast drive. The “5” in the name stands for, you guessed it, Thunderbolt 5, which, despite being announced seemingly forever ago, has been painfully slow to trickle into the market. This made testing a bit tricky, but fortunately a friend let me borrow his brand-new MacBook Pro 14 for testing. The results were impressive.

LaCie claims read/write speeds of up to 6,700 MB/s and 5,300 MB/s, which it says are adequate for real-time editing of 8K and 6K RAW footage. In testing the highest speeds, file transfers were 5,787 MB/s read and 5,188 MB/s write—which, while not quite matching the claim, still make it far and away the fastest drive in this guide. But raw speeds are just numbers for spreadsheets; I was more interested in real-world performance. I threw some 6K ProRes RAW at the Pro5 and was able to edit it on the MacBook Pro in DaVinci Resolve Studio.

The downside here is the price. It started at $600 for the 4-TB version (the minimum you’d want for working with ProRes RAW video files). That was already pricey, but these days that’s climbed to insane heights ($1,600 as of this update), making it a less compelling value. Still, if you need the speed, this is the drive to get.

Best Padded Drive

Samsung's T9 has been my go-to portable drive for a couple of years now. While I like the LaCie drives that usually dominate this category, the Samsung is plenty fast, clocking in at over 1,350 MB/s and handily beating the Crucial X9. The T9 also seems to draw less power, or at least when I plug it into my Android tablet, it drains the battery far less than any other drive I use regularly.

The padding on the T9 is less substantial than the LaCie's, but it's also considerably cheaper and has held up well to life on the road. The only catch is that it's not waterproof or dustproof. The padding stops on the ends, so it’s not completely sealed. I haven’t had any issues, but if you get it wet, it will be a problem. If you’re worried about that, check out the T7 Shield below.

  • Samsung T7 Shield 2-TB SSD for approximately $575: This drive is very similar to the T9, but it has an IP65 rating, which means it’s safe in the rain and protected from dust and sand. The T7 line has built-in security features like hardware-based encryption, but unlike the Touch model, the Shield doesn't have a fingerprint reader.

The Best DIY Drive Enclosure

With hard drive prices skyrocketing, repurposing an internal NVMe SSD you already own for an external drive is a compelling alternative. Plenty of DIY drive enclosures are available, with some promising speeds up to 80 GBps (with compatible USB 4 ports). The D1 SSD comes in two flavors: the 80-GBps Pro drive I tested and a slower 40-GBps Plus version, which makes more sense if you don’t have USB 4 (there's also a base 10-GBps option that's much slower but cheaper). If you do, though, this is an incredibly fast drive, and thanks to the heat-dissipating design, it never throttled on me.

The D1 SSD Pro supports the full suite of USB specs, from 2.x up to USB 4, plus Thunderbolt 4 and 5. In addition to a USB 4 port on your computer, you'll need a PCIe 4 or 5 SSD inside the enclosure to reach top speeds; expect speeds around 6,500 MB/s for sequential read/write (the CrystalDiskMark benchmark score was 6,597 for read and 6,239 for write). It’s also plenty fast in the real world, having no trouble serving up 4K clips for my DaVinci Resolve Studio video editing test.

If your PC can support it and you have an internal SSD that can take advantage of it, this is the fastest external hard drive setup I've tested.

  • Satechi DotDisk 80Gbps NVMe SSD Enclosure for $200: One problem with making SSDs portable is that you can't ignore thermodynamics. A tiny case is great for your pocket, but terrible for dumping heat. Most small, no-name SSD cases I've tried get hot enough to burn skin. Satechi's DotDisk is the first 80-Gbps SSD enclosure I've tried that can actually stay cool. It's tiny, too. At 3.9 inches by 1.4 inches and just 0.7 inches thick, it's plenty pocketable, and with a drive in it, it weighs just 4 ounces. It's by far the most portable USB 4- and Thunderbolt 5-capable enclosure I've tried, and it stays cool enough to touch while delivering great performance, making it well worth the money if portability is your top priority.

Best SSD for Your NAS Server

Most of the NAS servers we recommend still use mechanical drives. This is partly because they're cheaper, and partly because SSDs aren't great at constantly writing data, which is what you tend to do with a NAS. That's where Sandisk's NAS 800 drive comes in. The NAS 800 drive—available in 960 GB, 1.92 TB, 3.84 TB, and 7.68 TB—is optimized for exactly this use case. It also does an admirable job of staying cool compared to more consumer-oriented drives.

The NAS 800 has a staggering rating of 14 petabytes written (PBW, a measurement of the total data amount written over its lifespan). The five-year warranty says you can write the full 7.67 TB of data to the drive every day, for five years, which is impressive even if the longevity is short (it's unlikely most users will be doing this). I look forward to some of these making their way into BackBlaze's hard drive stats in the next year to see how well this claim holds up. It's worth noting that, given memory costs, the 7.68-TB model is currently $2,750 (up from its launch price one month ago at $2,200).

Performance here is quite good, especially on the cooling front. During large data transfers and large numbers of small file transfers between a Linux laptop and a TerraMaster NAS, this drive ran noticeably cooler than the WD Black and Blue drives next to it (about 15 to 20 degrees Fahrenheit cooler).

Best Gaming Drive

Take this category with a grain of salt. Most of the drives here will work just fine for gaming (stick with the fastest you can afford). That said, Western Digital’s P40 does have cool RGB lights on the bottom if that’s your jam. In my testing, the lights didn’t seem to impact power consumption.

As for performance, my tests were inconsistent. This drive is capable of speeds that handily beat both the Envoy Pro and Samsung T7, but at other times it seemed to bog down (at least in benchmarks). In real-world use, the bottleneck I consistently hit was some lag in transferring huge amounts of data. That might be a deal-breaker for some, but for the price, it remains a solid choice.

Best Bare Drive

If you want to put a bigger SSD in your laptop or an enclosure, all you need is a bare drive, which is generally cheaper than the external drives recommended above. First, figure out what type of drive your PC uses (most new Macs don't let you upgrade internal components). Consult your manufacturer’s documentation to find out. These days, the most common form factor is M.2 2280, the long, thin drive shown in the image above. More compact laptops may use a similar, but shorter, M.2 2242 design. There are also older SSDs that use the legacy SATA interface, but these are slower than NVMe variants. Again, check your PC to confirm the drive it needs before you buy.

The Samsung 990 PRO SSD NVMe achieved a read speed of 7,458 MB/s in my testing, more or less matching the claimed 7,450 MBs/6,900 MBs read/write speeds. If you’re doing a lot of drive-intensive tasks, like editing video or gaming, this drive is worth the money. The largest capacity you can get is 4 TB, and the price is reasonable considering the speed (amazingly, the version with a heatsink is even cheaper). There are faster options, but you’ll pay for them, and I find that currently, beyond this drive, there is a diminishing return in the speed versus price curve. I’ve been using the 990 PRO SSD as my main drive for several months now, and it works great for editing 5.2K video footage and compiling software. My favorite part? It generates very little heat.

  • Sandisk WD_Black SN850X 1-TB SSD for $244: Another fast one, Sandisk claims up to 7,300 MB/s read speeds, and in benchmark tests, it came close. Like the Samsung above, to take full advantage of the speed here, you’ll need a system that supports the PCIe 4.0 SSD standard, but this is a great drive if you want to upgrade a gaming system, whether it’s a desktop PC or your PlayStation 5. This drive is also one of the few I’ve seen that’s available up to 8-TB capacity.
  • Samsung 990 Evo Plus 2-TB SSD for $580: The 990 EVO Plus is an upgrade to the very popular 990 EVO. The original didn't offer anything compelling and never made it into this guide, but the new version is impressively fast and not overly hot, unlike many Gen 5 PCIe drives I’ve tested. The 990 EVO Plus also launched with a 4-TB model, something missing the first time around. In terms of speed, it doesn’t quite match the WD_Black SN850X, topping out at 5,677 MB/s read, but it’s fast enough for most uses and remains quite cool even when pushed. If you’re looking for a good all-around drive, this one is a good choice, though it is on the pricey side for what you get. Keep an eye out for when it goes on sale.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Happened to WD_Black Drives?

The short answer is that the HDD versions appear to be sticking around, but the SSDs are being rebranded. For a long time, Western Digital and SanDisk were the same company. Recently, the two split, and WD Blue and WD_Black are now split between the two companies, with Western Digital taking the large, spinning-drive portion of the brands and SanDisk taking the SSDs. SanDisk (now stylized as Sandisk) is in the process of rebranding its SSDs from WD_Black to Optimus GX and Optimus GX Pro. I’ll be testing both as the new models become available.

Which Hard Drive Is Right for Me?

Picking the right hard drive comes down to balancing three things: speed, size, and price. If you’re making nightly backups, then speed probably doesn't matter. Go for the cheapest drive you can find—up to a point. Drives don’t last forever, but some last longer than others. I suggest sticking with known brands with a good reputation, such as Seagate, Western Digital, Samsung, and the others featured here. This is based partly on experience and partly on drive-failure data Backblaze has published for years. Backblaze goes through massive amounts of hard drives backing up customers’ data, and its report is worth reading. The takeaway is simple: Stick with names you know.

Which External Hard Drive Brands Are Most Reliable?

This is difficult to answer, as it depends on too many factors. But according to Backblaze's 2025 stats report, the best drive makers are Toshiba, Seagate, Western Digital, and Hitachi (HGST in Backblaze's charts, now owned by Western Digital). The current best-performing drives appear to be Seagate's 6- and 8-TB SSDs. With that in mind, if I were building a network-attached storage (NAS) system, I'd use the Seagate Exos 8 TB HDD. After that, though, failures—especially among SSDs—appear pretty random.

Which Is Better, SSD or HDD?

It depends on what you’re doing. If you need fast data transfer speeds, then you want a solid-state drive (SSD). If you have massive amounts of data to store or back up, then a spinning drive (hybrid hard drive, or HDD) is the cheaper option. If you’re a videographer, you need both—open your wallet wide. In general, SSDs are the way to go when you can afford it.

If speed trumps price, then you want to look at the solid-state drives we’ve listed here. SSDs don’t just have a speed advantage. They also lack moving parts, so they’ll withstand bumps and drops better than spinning drives. The disadvantage is that they can wear out faster. Every write operation to an SSD—that is, when you save something to it—slightly degrades the individual NAND cells that make up the drive, which wears it out somewhat faster than a spinning drive. Just how much faster depends on how you use it. That said, I have several SSDs that are more than five years old, and I’ve used them for daily backups throughout that time. None of them have had any problems.

Do you need an SSD over a spinning drive? The answer is almost always yes, but if you can afford it. They’re especially useful for any drive you use regularly: your main boot drive, an external drive you use to edit documents, and fast backups.

The one caveat is that if your Mac or PC doesn’t support the same USB standard as the external SSD you’re considering, then you might be wasting your money. A drive claiming USB 3.0 speeds in the neighborhood of 2,000 MB/s will do you no good if your laptop has only USB 2.0 ports. Check your laptop's specs, and don’t waste money on transfer speeds you’ll never achieve.

Another limitation is if you’re going to leave the drive off for long periods—think years, not weeks. In that case, SSDs can be more prone to data corruption, so traditional hard drives (or tape drives) are a better choice. For most casual users, though, this will not be an issue.

Which Backup Software Should You Use?

The answer depends on whether you’re using macOS, Windows, Linux, Android, or iOS. Unfortunately, there is no one solution for everything. We suggest using one (or two) of the storage devices above, plus some kind of cloud storage backup. That way, even if your drives fail, your data is still backed up in the cloud or on a redundant hard drive. See our complete guide to backing up your digital life for our top-pick backup solutions for every platform.

How We Test External Hard Drives

I test these drives by first running them through a suite of benchmarking tools. On Windows, I use CrystalDiskMark to measure both sequential read/write speeds and random read/write speeds. On macOS, I do the same with the Blackmagic Disk Speed Test and sometimes AmorphousDiskMark, and on Linux I use KDiskMark (and I usually reformat the disk from exFAT to ext4). I run tests six times and then take the average. In addition to benchmarks, I have two folders for testing real-world speeds. I transfer a 25-gigabyte folder of MP3 files, then a folder with three files that together total 25 gigabytes. For top-end drives, I also test read and write speeds for ProRes RAW video files.

After I run the tests, I use the drive in day-to-day tasks—editing files directly off it (booting from it for bare drives), making nightly backups, tossing it in my camera bag, and so on. All these data points, along with price, form factor, portability, and other functionality (does it offer encryption, etc.), go into informing the decisions about which disk is best.

entries.title: Bose Launches New Wired Earbuds After More Than a Decade
entries.summary: The Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are the first new wired headphones from the brand since 2015, inspired directly by teen preferences. We got an early listen.
entries.content:
Bose used to make lots of wired headphones. But it’s been a minute. Specifically, it’s been 11 years. Since then, wired headphones entered 2026 having a serious moment, with sales up for the first time in five years—10 percent in the back half of 2025 and 20 percent at the start of 2026. Young people are driving the trend, including celebrities sporting wired earbuds and literally writing songs about them.

Bose president of consumer audio Raza Haider (among others at the company) noticed. He dropped off his teen at college last year and saw wired earbuds left and right. A return to wired earbuds seems to be a national trend—it’s certainly popular among the Gen Z and Gen A of New York City, and the teenage kids of WIRED staffers too.

The new $99 Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds come to the market just in time to capitalize on this trend. Launching them, from idea to final product, took the company around eight or nine months, said Haider. This is much faster than most audio releases I’m familiar with. Haider explained that Bose has been working toward enabling faster, more efficient production to accelerate new product launches, revisions, and collaborations.

Testing the Bose Wired Earbuds: Are They Any Good?

I was one of a few reviewers to get these earbuds ahead of launch. I’ve had them for only four days, and they’re technically a late-stage prototype, not the final product, so this is more of an impression than a full review. But so far, so good.

As with any wired headphones, the simplicity is a big part of the appeal. There’s no battery to charge, no app to download, no Bluetooth to fiddle with, and no latency to ruin your TV show or video game.

Already, the Bose earbuds leapfrog cheaper wired pairs (like Apple EarPods) in sound quality and active noise canceling (ANC). They have clear detail across lows, mids, and highs, especially for something at this price point. More importantly, the noise canceling is a godsend. I can listen to music at more comfortable levels, even during a commute or café stop.

What I don’t love: The central control panel is a little heavy. It has a volume up and volume down, as well as a play/pause/noise-canceling mode switch button, but it weighs down the cable. It’s pretty flush against my torso, which is nice, but it also weighs down the earbuds in my ears. The cable tension it adds is annoying, especially compared to the tension-free experience of using wireless earbuds. The cable is thick and premium-feeling, but it inevitably ends up tangled inside of the included soft pouch.

The earbuds have (removable) silicone wing-tip stabilizers, and the box comes with extra ear tip and stabilizer sizes to find your best fit. The buds come in black, white, and a limited-edition mint color, and they start shipping October 15. You can preorder starting today at Bose and Best Buy.

While Bose's return to wired headphones feels significant, wired earbuds never truly went away. Here are some of WIRED's favorites that are currently available to buy.

entries.title: OpenAI Pauses Training Its Most Powerful Models After Rogue Agents Target Government
entries.summary: Sam Altman says the company “have not been as fast as we would have liked” at dealing with security breaches, after news of further incidents over the summer forces another temporary halt.
entries.content:
OpenAI said it has paused training its most powerful artificial intelligence models as incidents of agents breaching websites’ security controls or posting to third-party sites continue to pile up. On Friday, OpenAI said it had notified “dozens” of bodies, including governments, universities, and public agencies, who might have been impacted by its models’ activities on the internet during training and evaluation.

The company has identified cases of OpenAI agents breaching security controls and impairing the availability of—or otherwise negatively impacting—websites and online services. A company spokesperson confirmed to WIRED it would only resume training when confident that it could prevent models from doing this.

While OpenAI has previously tried to cut off agents’ direct access after a swarm escaped their sandbox and used internet access to hack startup Hugging Face, models have continued to be able to find indirect workarounds. “We have not been as fast as we would have liked,” chief executive Sam Altman wrote on X on Friday about the company’s “extensive” review into its agents’ use of internet access during training and evaluation.

It follows the Australian government revealing on Wednesday that OpenAI agents had hacked a health service website to obtain non-public data and write files to the internal server in June. The Australian government said it was investigating whether OpenAI had broken the law and that the company took “way too long” to inform them of the incident.

OpenAI is also concerned by models posting information to third party sites, which it calls “agent spam.” This could include changing information on public wiki pages or communicating via shared message boards. Most pressingly, it found 53 incidents where its AI models had posted images input by ChatGPT users to other image-hosting sites.

Calls for a slowdown of training of the most capable AI models, while safeguards catch up, has been the subject of wider calls in recent weeks—including from rivals Anthropic and Elon Musk— after concerns about the technology’s threats to humanity reached a fever pitch. “This is not the first time we have hit pause to take such measures, nor do we expect it will be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

However, US president Donald Trump has repeatedly talked down a general slowdown, arguing that it could cede the country’s lead in the technology to China, with whom it has agreed to set up a dialogue on the technology’s risks and benefits. In an interview with Fox News ahead of his dinner with Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei on Sunday night, he again brushed off concerns about AI agents going rogue: “I don’t worry about it,” he said.

entries.title: Space Lasers Are About to Get Their First Real Test Generating Energy
entries.summary: Startup Star Catcher is launching a system that, if successful, would be the first time energy has been beamed between two separate spacecraft.
entries.content:
Google, SpaceX, and a host of startups are all planning to build data centers in space. But for those plans to work, they’ll need power. Lots of it.

Star Catcher, a startup based in Jacksonville, Florida, aims to provide it by concentrating the sun’s energy and using lasers to beam it to satellites’ waiting solar panels. The company is preparing to launch its prototype system aboard a SpaceX rocket this week that will transmit energy to another satellite in orbit.

If it’s successful, it would be the first time lasers have beamed energy between two untethered objects in space. But the idea of generating solar power in space goes back decades.

It showed up in a 1941 sci-fi piece by Isaac Asimov, and NASA studied it in the 1970s. “Launching large amounts of hardware into orbit was extremely expensive, so generating power in space and transmitting it elsewhere rarely made practical sense,” says Hanieh Fattahi, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light. But now, falling launch costs are making it more feasible to have orbital industries that will be able to provide such energy.

“There isn't a power grid in space,” says chief executive officer and cofounder Andrew Rush. “Everybody just goes on these little camping trips.”

Star Catcher’s solution is an array of what it calls power nodes that serve as both a solar power plant and power line. To generate energy, the firm’s satellites gather sunlight using a collection of lenses and refine it into the wavelengths of light that Star Catcher says can provide up to 10 times more power than diffuse sunlight. It then emits a laser beam—think of it as an ethereal transmission cable—that can be directed at satellites in need of power. That promises more uptime and, Rush says, more profit for satellite operators.

In a world where launches cost thousands of dollars per kilogram of weight, reducing battery size while adding more useful instruments—or in the case of space data centers, GPUs—can pay dividends.

There’s clear interest in what Star Catcher is offering. The company announced a $65 million round of funding earlier this year, and it won a $30 million award from the US Space Force. The company has also inked 40 letters of intent from prospective buyers and, more importantly, 10 power purchase agreements, which are long-term contracts. There’s also a sign of optimism for space-based industries launching on the same SpaceX mission as Star Catcher’s system: Google’s first attempt at a space-based data center is also hitching a ride on the rocket.

The satellite launching this week, dubbed Protostar, is a small-scale version of the satellites Star Catcher hopes to eventually deploy that Rush says will provide “meaningful commercial power provisioning services in orbit before the end of the decade.” But it’ll be the first time the entire system comes together in space, with the company using its tracking technology to beam energy to an untethered cubesat that’s launching at the same time.

“Part of this demonstration is testing how much power is received by the cubesat as it moves away from Protostar and comparing that against our models,” says Rush.

The company has done a space-based test of its technology that would allow it to track satellites it’s transmitting energy to, and it set a record last year for beaming power on the ground, besting a mark set by DARPA.

That test delivered more than 1 kilowatt of power to off-the-shelf solar panels—enough juice to power a microwave. That means there’s a ways to go to power telecommunications satellites, let alone space-based data centers, but Rush says the proof-of-concept on the ground is what gives him confidence that the company is ready to see what it can do in orbit. He says Star Catcher is still in the “crawl” phase but on its way to walking, then running.

This won’t be the first test of lasers in space. The Naval Research Laboratory completed an experiment in 2023, operating a space laser to generate power for 100 days. However, the system was a single unit, and the beam traveled less than 5 feet. (If Star Catcher is working on crawling, then this experiment was akin to tummy time.) That laser only operated with 11 percent efficiency, an issue Fattahi says will need to be overcome. She also says tracking systems, managing heat, and ensuring equipment can operate in the cold vacuum of space for years also need to be teased out to make space-based lasers economically viable.

Researchers have also explored other forms of space-based solar, including successful tests by Caltech scientists to transmit solar power via microwaves back to Earth. That technique can transmit more energy, but it requires a massive receiver to harness it, whereas lasers can hit a much smaller target.

“As we grow the infrastructure in space,” Rush says of Star Catcher’s satellites, “we begin to make it more economical to put larger and more capable industry in space. I view what we're building as transformational for the space sector as reusable launch vehicles.”

entries.title: Best Apple Watch: Series 12, Ultra 4, and SE 3 (2026)
entries.summary: From the latest Ultra to last year’s SE, these are the Apple Watches worth considering.
entries.content:
As WIRED’s resident wearable tester, I’ve tried enough smartwatches to know there’s life beyond the Apple Watch. I just apparently don’t want it. Maybe it’s because I joined the Apple ecosystem at 10 years old and have been indoctrinated ever since. I’m fluent in iOS, macOS, and watchOS, and for better or worse, the Apple Watch is my default wearable.

But what’s the best Apple Watch to buy? There are now three models, each with its own set of features, and the differences between them can appear minor even when the prices aren’t. Fortunately, I’ve tested them all; Here’s how the current lineup stacks up.

For more recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Apple Watch Bands, the Best Apple Watch Accessories, and the Best Smartwatches.

Featured in This Guide

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Best Apple Watch Overall

The Series 12 is Apple’s flagship watch. Its biggest upgrade is the new Health Sensing System, which improves the breadth, accuracy, and frequency of its health tracking. The ECG now uses 32 electrodes for better skin contact, up from two on the Series 11, while improved optical sensing and more efficient LEDs deliver more accurate heart-rate readings. The Series 12 also tracks your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day and HRV as often as every five minutes, compared with every five minutes for heart rate and roughly every two hours for HRV on the Series 11.

The Series 12 also introduces Apple’s Readiness score, which gives you a snapshot of how prepared your body is for the day based on your recent health and activity data. Audio Intelligence is another major addition, though two of its headline features (Live Rewind and Siri Recap) won’t arrive until later this year.

Battery life remains rated for up to 24 hours, but charging is faster. Fifteen minutes delivers up to 12 hours of normal use, and five minutes get you up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. Just about the only feature the Series 11 lacks is satellite connectivity, but if you don't go off the grid, then it has everything else you need.

Specs
Case(s) 42 mm or 46 mm
Display Wide-angle OLED, Always-on Retina display, up to 2,000 nits
Battery Life Up to 24 hours (up to 38 hours in Low Power Mode)
GPS Precision L1 GPS
Finishes Aluminum: Dark Bronze, Light Gold, Black, Space Gray; Titanium: Radiant Gold, Natural; Ceramic: Pearl White, Night Blue

Best Battery Life

The Ultra 4’s biggest upgrades are its longer battery life, faster charging, and new health-tracking capabilities. It lasts up to 50 hours on a charge—up from 42 hours on the Ultra 3—and up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode. Fast charging gets a boost, with 15 minutes on the charger providing up to 18 hours of normal use and five minutes offering up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. A new Health Sensing System and faster S11 chip enable frequent background heart-rate and HRV tracking, the Readiness score, and Apple’s suite of Audio Intelligence features.

Beyond those improvements, the Ultra 4 is essentially the same smartwatch as its predecessor. It remains built for multi-day hikes, water sports, and endurance activities, with water resistance up to 100 meters and a depth gauge rated to 40 meters for recreational scuba diving. Its standout feature remains satellite messaging, which lets you contact emergency services when you’re beyond cellular or Wi-Fi coverage. Fall and crash detection, plus a built-in siren, offer additional precautions to get help when you need it.

My biggest complaint is that the 49-mm can be too large on slimmer wrists. I’d like a 46-mm option.

Specs
Case(s) 49 mm
Display Wide-angle OLED, Always-on Retina display, up to 3,000 nits
Battery Life Up to 50 hours (up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode)
GPS Precision dual-frequency GPS
Finishes Titanium: Natural, Black

Best Budget-Friendly Apple Watch

Apple didn’t update the SE this year, so the Watch SE (3rd Gen) remains the most affordable. It’s designed with the S10 chip, which enables many of the health features the SE 2 lacked, such as sleep apnea notifications and skin temperature sensing. It’s compatible with watchOS 27, so you can use the dynamic app grid, the Siri app, and Workout Buddy. It has fast charging, and even though it doesn’t have the Series 12’s 24-hour battery life, former WIRED editor Adrienne So still somehow managed to eke out a full day with it, even with the always-on display.

The screen is only a 1,000-nit display compared to the 2,000-nit display on the Series 11’s wide-angle OLED display, and it doesn't have the UWB locator chip. You’re missing out on the new features, including the new Readiness score, high-frequency heart-rate and HRV tracking, and Audio Intelligence. It also cannot check your blood oxygen or take an electrocardiogram, nor does it have the latest hypertension notifications.

Specs
Case(s) 40 mm or 44 mm (aluminum)
Display OLED, Always-on Retina display, up to 1,000 nits
Battery Life Up to 18 hours (up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode)
GPS GPS
Finishes Aluminum: Starlight, Midnight

Compare Top 3 Apple Watches

Product Case Size(s) Material(s) Display GPS Battery Life Price

Honorable Mentions

Apple Watch Series 11 for $399: With no price difference between generations, the Series 11 only makes sense if you find it at a significant discount. It misses out on high-frequency background heart-rate tracking, Recovery HRV readings, the Readiness score, and Apple’s suite of Audio Intelligence tools. It also uses standard GPS instead of the newer Precision L1 GPS, and it lacks the latest fast-charging boost, but it can still charge for up to eight hours of battery life in 15 minutes.

Apple Watch Ultra 3 for $799: With no price difference between generations, the Ultra 3 only makes sense if you find it at a significant discount. It has a shorter battery life, rated for up to 42 hours compared with the Ultra 4’s 50 hours. You also miss out on Audio Intelligence, high-frequency heart-rate and HRV tracking, and the Readiness score. Otherwise, it’s basically the same outdoor-focused Apple Watch.

Avoid These Apple Watches

WatchOS 27 only works with the Series 9 and newer, so I wouldn’t recommend buying an Apple Watch older than that. With less price variation between generations, I’d also only consider an older Apple Watch if it’s on sale.

How I Test Apple Watches

For my initial reviews, I wear each Apple Watch day and night for about a week, using it as I would a typical smartwatch, fitness tracker, and sleep tracker. Afterward, I continue testing for at least another month to evaluate longer-term claims and how useful its wellness data proves to be in practice.

I sport each watch during workouts, throughout the day, and while sleeping to judge its comfort over time. I also consider screen readability indoors and outdoors, and the responsiveness of the touchscreen and physical controls. I test everyday functions like Siri, music playback, and watchOS to evaluate how intuitive they are to navigate and how well they integrate with the iPhone experience. I track how long the battery lasts with features such as workout tracking, notifications, and sleep tracking enabled. I also note charging speed and how practical it is to maintain throughout a full day and overnight.

Because the Apple Watch is also a fitness tracker, I use it for a range of activities, including but not limited to runs, rides, and strength training. I compare heart rate readings, workout detection, step counts, and other fitness metrics against previous Apple Watches and competitors (i.e., Oura and Whoop). I also compare sleep tracking with predecessors and competitors, looking at the quality of the data, how useful the metrics are, and whether it provides actionable insights.
